title: What about tomorrow? — the future and the weather
goal: Talk about plans and the weather forecast — learn the future tense, and the one important place where Bosnian uses the present instead.
bekal: forming the future with *ću / ćeš / će* + dictionary form, including the negative
talking about the weather with sentences that have no subject

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kakvo će biti vrijeme?
dialogs.intro: Thursday evening in the apartment kitchen. Budi has heard about the mountains around Sarajevo and wants to climb one.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Emire, kakvo će biti vrijeme sutra?
lines.id: Emir, what's the weather going to be like tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Emir:
lines.text: Pogledat ću na telefonu. Bit će sunčano i toplo, oko dvadeset.
lines.id: I'll check on my phone. Sunny and warm, about twenty degrees.
lines.literal: look I-will on phone-loc. be it-will sunny-n and warm-n, about twenty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Odlično! Onda ćemo ići na Bjelašnicu?
lines.id: Great! So we'll go to Bjelašnica?
lines.literal: excellent! then we-will go to Bjelašnica-acc?

lines.speaker: Emir:
lines.text: Nećemo sutra — sutra radim. Možemo u nedjelju.
lines.id: Not tomorrow — I'm working tomorrow. We can go on Sunday.
lines.literal: we-won't tomorrow — tomorrow I-work. we-can on Sunday-acc.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Važi. A kada počinje zima ovdje?
lines.id: Deal. And when does winter start here?
lines.literal: it-holds. and when it-starts winter here?

lines.speaker: Emir:
lines.text: Krajem novembra obično padne prvi snijeg. U decembru je već hladno.
lines.id: The first snow usually falls at the end of November. By December it's already cold.
lines.literal: end-ins November-gen usually it-falls first-m snow. in December-loc it-is already cold-n.

lines.speaker: Emir:
lines.text: Minus deset, ponekad minus petnaest. Ali suho je, nije kao kiša.
lines.id: Minus ten, sometimes minus fifteen. But it's dry, not like rain.
lines.literal: minus ten, sometimes minus fifteen. but dry-n it-is, not-it-is like rain.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: U Jakarti nikad nije bilo ispod dvadeset pet.
lines.id: In Jakarta it never got below twenty-five.
lines.literal: in Jakarta-loc never not-it-is been-n below twenty five.

lines.speaker: Emir:
lines.text: Onda ćeš se smrznuti. Trebat će ti dobra jakna i kapa.
lines.id: Then you'll freeze. You'll need a good jacket and a hat.
lines.literal: then you-will self freeze. need it-will to-you good-f jacket and hat.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kupit ću sve u oktobru. Obećavam.
lines.id: I'll buy everything in October. I promise.
lines.literal: buy I-will all in October-loc. I-promise.

lines.speaker: Emir:
lines.text: Nećeš. Svi to kažu, pa kupe u januaru.
lines.id: You won't. Everyone says that, then they buy in January.
lines.literal: you-won't. all that they-say, then they-buy in January-loc.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vidjet ćemo! Kada dođe novembar, javit ću ti.
lines.id: We'll see! When November comes, I'll let you know.
lines.literal: see we-will! when it-comes November, let-know I-will to-you.

notes: **Two ways to write the future, both in this dialogue.** *Pogledat ću* — the verb comes first, its final *-i* is cut off, then *ću* stands on its own. *Onda ćemo ići* — the helping verb comes first and the verb stays whole. Both mean the same and both are correct; all that decides it is what's sitting in first place.

***Kada dođe novembar, javit ću ti* — notice the present tense.** After *kada* (when) and *ako* (if), Bosnian uses the **present**, not the future, even when the meaning is clearly future. That's exactly what English does (*when November comes*). Note too that the verb is the *svršeni* (perfective) form — *dođe*, not *dolazi* — as covered in Unit 15.

***Nećemo sutra* — the negative future uses a fused form.** *Neću, nećeš, neće, nećemo, nećete, neće*. And unlike the positive form, here the verb is **never cut short**: *neću raditi*, not *neću radit*.

***Krajem novembra* = "toward the end of November".** A frozen instrumental used as a time expression, related to *početkom* (at the beginning) and *sredinom* (in the middle): *početkom maja*, *sredinom godine*. The month that follows is in the genitive.

**Bjelašnica and Jahorina** are the two mountains where the skiing events of the 1984 Winter Olympics were held — both less than an hour from central Sarajevo. It's one of the least-known things about the city: you can have coffee in the old town in the morning and be standing in snow before noon.

grammars.title: Futur I — the future tense
body: It's formed from the short form of *htjeti* (want) plus the dictionary form. Because the short form is a little word, it follows the second-place rule you've known since Unit 12.
after: **Two word orders, one meaning.** If the verb comes first, the final *-i* of the dictionary form is cut off and *ću* follows: *radit ću, kupit ću, vidjet ćemo, bit će*. If another word is in first place, the verb stays whole at the end: *Ja ću raditi. Sutra ćemo kupiti karte.* Verbs ending in *-ći* are never cut short: *ići ću, doći će, reći ćemo*.

**In Serbia the two are often written as one word — *radiću, kupiću*.** You'll also see that form in eastern Bosnia and in a lot of online writing. This course uses the separate form, which is usual in Sarajevo and in Croatia. They sound exactly the same; only the spelling differs.
**Questions use the long form:** *Hoćeš li doći?* — and so do short answers: *Hoću* (yes, I will) or *Neću* (no). *Da li ćeš doći?* is equally correct.

**The present often stands in for the future** when there's a clear time expression: *Sutra idem u Mostar.* *U nedjelju radim.* This is very common in conversation — just like English "I'm going to Mostar tomorrow". If you're unsure of the future form, this is always a safe option.

grammars.title: Vrijeme — the weather, and sentences with no subject
body: Almost all Bosnian weather sentences have no subject at all: just an adjective in the **neuter** form plus *je*.
after: **The adjective is always neuter** because there's no noun for it to follow: *hladno je*, not *hladan je*. The same pattern is used for situations in general: *lijepo je ovdje* (it's nice here), *teško je* (it's hard), *jasno je* (it's clear).

***Pada kiša* does have a subject, and it's the rain itself** — literally "rain is falling". So the past form follows *kiša*, which is feminine: *Padala je kiša.* For snow, which is masculine: *Padao je snijeg.*

***Vrijeme* means weather **and** time.** *Nemam vremena* (I don't have time) and *Lijepo je vrijeme* (the weather is nice) use the same word. Context tells them apart, and it's never really confusing.

**Forecast phrases you'll hear on the radio:** *Sutra se očekuje kiša* (rain is expected tomorrow), *Temperatura od pet do dvanaest stepeni*, *Ujutro magla, poslije podne sunčano*. You don't need to produce them — recognizing them is enough.

blocks.text: Bosnian month names are almost the same as the English ones — both borrowed from Latin. This is one of the cheapest lists you'll learn in the whole course.

In **Croatia** the month names are completely different and come from old Slavic: *siječanj, veljača, ožujak, travanj, svibanj, lipanj, srpanj, kolovoz, rujan, listopad, studeni, prosinac*. You'll see them on Croatian tickets, newspapers and timetables, so it's good to know the list exists — but in Bosnia, the international names are used.

Dates use **ordinal numbers**, just as English says "the fifth". To give today's date, use the ordinary form — *Danas je peti maj* (today is the fifth of May). To say "on the …", use the **genitive**, and the month goes into the genitive too — *petog maja*, *petnaestog juna*, *prvog septembra*. In writing, dates use periods, day first: **15. 6. 2026.**

blocks.title: Two dates to know in Bosnia
items: **1 March** — Independence Day (*Dan nezavisnosti*), and **25 November** — Statehood Day (*Dan državnosti*). Both are public holidays in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Islamic holidays follow the Hijri calendar, so their dates move every year: *Ramazanski bajram* (Eid al-Fitr) and *Kurban-bajram* (Eid al-Adha). The greeting: *Bajram šerif mubarek olsun*, answered with *Allah razi olsun* — two Turkish phrases that have survived intact in Bosnia. A simpler greeting that's always safe: *Sretan Bajram!*

items: What will the weather be like tomorrow?
Tomorrow will be sunny and warm.
I'll buy a jacket in October.
When November comes, I'll let you know.
